step_results: Done! The script counts the orders and reports there are **32 orders** in data/orders.json. The script uses the `log()` function from src/log.js as required by your project guidelines.
Done! The script displays the top 3 customers by total spend in euros. Dana Ruiz leads with €538.08 in total orders.
Done! The script shows revenue per month in chronological order. September had significantly higher revenue (€970.67) compared to July and August (around €183 each).
Done! The validation script confirms all 32 orders are valid—no problems found. Each order has a proper id, customer name, numeric amount, and YYYY-MM-DD formatted date.

Done! I've updated `loadOrders` to accept an optional second argument with a `debug` flag. When debug is true, it logs the number of orders loaded and the file path. The function maintains backward compatibility—existing code works as before.
Done! The script calculates the average order value for non-refund orders as €51.20.

Done! The script exports all orders as CSV with a header row and properly quoted customer names. The first 10 lines show the header and 9 sample orders with their IDs, customer names, amounts (in cents), and dates.
Done! The search script works correctly. It finds customers case-insensitively and displays matching orders, or prints "no matches" if there are no results.

Done! The formatEuros function formats cents as euros with thousands separators and proper negative handling. The demo shows it handles various cases correctly—large amounts, small amounts, negatives, and zero.
Done! The script finds and displays the largest order (O-1022 from Dana Ruiz for €156.00 on 2026-09-10) with all its fields nicely formatted.
Done! The daily report shows 32 orders with total revenue of €1,337.92, and the best day was 2026-09-10 with €190.99 in revenue.
Done! The script lists the 3 refunds (each for €49.00) with customer names and a total refunded of €147.00.
Done! The script outputs all 8 distinct customers sorted alphabetically in pretty JSON format, ready to paste into other tools.
Done! The benchmark shows loadOrders() averages 0.0171 ms per call over 1000 iterations—very efficient for reading the orders file.
